blocks.text: The previous lessons built, walked and edited **singly** linked lists. Doubly linked and circular lists use the same ideas with **more pointers to keep right**. A doubly linked insert or delete has to fix the links in **both directions**; a circular list has no null, so its edits must keep the ring **closed**. This lesson shows each operation step by step.

blocks.alt: Inserting 25 between 20 and 30 in a doubly linked list takes four pointer changes, numbered in a safe order. 1: the new node's prev points back to 20. 2: the new node's next points on to 30. 3: 30's prev, which pointed at 20, now points back to 25. 4: 20's next, which pointed at 30, now points on to 25. The two old links between 20 and 30 are drawn dashed.

blocks.text: 1. Doubly linked list: insert at a position

Walk to the node **before** the gap, `curr`. Then set the new node's own pointers first (**prev** to curr, **next** to curr's old next) — at that point nothing in the list has changed, so nothing can be lost. Then point the two neighbours at it: the old next's **prev**, and curr's **next** last. Inserting at index 0 is the special case: the new node becomes the head and its prev stays null.

blocks.caption: Watch the four pointers change in order: the new node's two first, then the neighbours.

blocks.code:
def insert_at(head, index, val):
    node = Node(val)
    if index == 0:                        # the new node becomes the head
        node.next = head
        if head is not None:
            head.prev = node
        return node
    curr = head
    for _ in range(index - 1):            # the node before the gap
        curr = curr.next
    node.prev = curr                      # 1. back to curr
    node.next = curr.next                 # 2. on to curr's old next
    if curr.next is not None:
        curr.next.prev = node             # 3. old next points back to it
    curr.next = node                      # 4. curr points on to it
    return head

blocks.text: **Time O(n)** to walk to the position, **O(1)** for the four pointer changes; **space O(1)**. At the front it's O(1) overall — and with a `tail` pointer, so is the end.
2. Doubly linked list: delete a node

This is where doubly linked lists pay off. To unlink a node from a **singly** linked list you need the node **before** it, which means a second walk. A doubly linked node already knows both neighbours: point its prev at its next, and its next back at its prev. If it was the head, the head moves on instead.

blocks.caption: Find the node, then two pointer changes unlink it — no second search for the node before it.

blocks.text: **Time O(n)** here only because we search by value; **unlinking is O(1)**. When you already hold the node — as an LRU cache does, through a hash map — the whole delete is O(1). That's the reason doubly linked lists exist.
3. Circular linked list: insert at the end in O(1)

A circular list is usually held by its **tail**, because `tail.next` is the head — both ends are one step away. To add a node at the end: point the new node at the head (`tail.next`), point the old tail at the new node, and the new node becomes the tail. An empty ring is the special case: a single node whose next is **itself**.

blocks.alt: A circular list 10, 20, 30 held by its tail, 30, whose next arrow curves back to the head, 10. A new node 40 is added after the tail: 40 points to the head, 30 points to 40, and 40 becomes the new tail.

blocks.caption: Two pointer changes and the tail moves: no walk at all.

blocks.code:
def insert_end(tail, val):           # the ring is held by its tail; tail.next is the head
    node = ListNode(val)
    if tail is None:                 # empty ring: one node pointing at itself
        node.next = node
        return node
    node.next = tail.next            # the new node points at the head
    tail.next = node                 # the old tail points at the new node
    return node                      # the new node is the new tail

blocks.text: **Time O(1), space O(1).** Inserting at the **front** is the same two pointer changes — the new node goes between the tail and the head either way — except you **keep the old tail** instead of returning the new node:

blocks.code:
def insert_front(tail, val):
    node = ListNode(val)
    if tail is None:
        node.next = node
        return node
    node.next = tail.next            # the new node points at the old head
    tail.next = node                 # the tail points at the new head
    return tail                      # the tail doesn't change

blocks.text: 4. Circular linked list: delete from the front
The head is `tail.next`, so removing it is one pointer change: the tail skips over it to the second node. The one-node ring is the special case — removing its only node leaves an empty ring.
**Time O(1), space O(1).** A circular list held by its tail is therefore a ready-made **queue**: add at the end, remove from the front, both O(1) — with one pointer instead of two.

blocks.alt: A cost table for the three types. Insert or delete at the front: O(1) for all three. Insert at the end: O(n) for singly without a tail pointer, O(1) for doubly with a tail pointer, O(1) for circular held by its tail. Delete at the end: O(n) for singly, O(1) for doubly, O(n) for circular. Delete a node you already hold: O(n) for singly, O(1) for doubly, O(n) for circular. Find a value: O(n) for all three.

elements.text: * O(1) if you also keep a tail pointer

items: **Doubly: updating only one direction** — after an insert or delete, every `a.next === b` must have `b.prev === a`. Check both.
**Doubly: overwriting `curr.next` too early** — set the new node's pointers first; change the neighbours last, or you lose the old next.
**Doubly: forgetting the head and tail** — deleting the head must move `head`, and the new head's `prev` must become null.
**Circular: leaving a null** — every edit must keep the ring closed; the new last node points at the head, never at null.
**Circular: the one-node ring** — a single node points at itself; inserting into an empty ring and deleting the last node are special cases.
A doubly linked insert sets **four** pointers and a delete changes **two** — in return, unlinking a node you hold is **O(1)**.
A circular list is best held by its **tail**: `tail.next` is the head, so adding at either end and removing from the front are all **O(1)**.
Edge cases decide correctness: the head, the tail, the empty list and the single node.
